narrator.voice: warm, unhurried, curious; a documentary voice that never oversells; speaks the dance's own words (names, counts) clearly
narrator.rule: The narrator only says what the profile says. Every sentence can be traced to a section, a claim or the music/movement DNA.
narrator.identity: one narrator for the whole atlas: the same face and animation everywhere; a native-speaker voice of the same character per language (studio-grade); the viewer chooses the language
narrator.wardrobe: in each episode the narrator wears the traditional apparel associated with the dance, reconstructed with meticulous care from the profile's costume notes and the licensed images — genuine and respectful, never a caricature; sacred, ceremonial or restricted attire is never worn (the narrator stays in neutral dress with a respectful nod in colour and fabric); the pack's visual_brief.wardrobe says which

scenes.title: Cold open
narration: In 1608, colonial lexicographer Diego González Holguín recorded the cachua as an ancient hand-holding Andean circle dance.
This is Cachua. 1788.
on_screen: Hero video, first 10 seconds (D-z-5_R9xS4)
Title card: Cachua · Peru · 1788

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The cachua dates back to the pre-Inca era and was practiced during the Inca period as a form of courtship.
In 1608, Diego González Holguín noted it in his vocabulary of the general language of Peru as a hand-holding dance.
Later, the style influenced colonial baroque music, appearing in Spanish-text villancicos with cachua rhythm sent to Charles IV of Spain around 1788 to 1790.
on_screen: Map: Peru · South America
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Occasions range from betrothals and Christmas celebrations to regional festivals like the Carnaval Chico de San Sebastián in Amantaní, Puno.
Historically and in contemporary contexts, it serves as a community celebration and courting ritual.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage — MISSING (use images)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The cachua is performed as a circle dance involving pairs.
Men strike the ground or rhythm with their shoes while women spin around their own axis.
In Amantaní, Puno, it is executed as a group Andean dance during local festivities.
Watch for shoe striking, axis spin.
on_screen: Hero video full screen, 30–45 s (D-z-5_R9xS4)
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: circle dance with pairs

scenes.title: Listen
narration: It is played in a rapid, unsyncopated two-four time signature, featuring a pattern where a quarter note alternates with two eighth notes across bars.
Melodies are traditionally pentatonic.
Listen for the quena, pan flute, drums, charango.
The pulse is 2/4.
Played in rapid unsyncopated two-four time with pentatonic melodies, featuring flutes like the quena and pan flute alongside drums, and sometimes charango or guitar.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Diego González Holguín, who documented the dance in 1608.
Found across the central and southern Andes of Peru, Bolivia, and Ecuador with differing local choreographies and instrumentations.
Directly descended from pre-Inca indigenous traditions, maintained through the Inca period, adapted into colonial baroque villancicos, and preserved today as a living Andean folk and circle dance.

music_brief.purpose: original soundtrack faithful to the tradition, with documented commercial reuse rights and no recurring royalties
music_brief.rights_rule: A composition brief does not clear an output. Record the provider/model/version, terms and date, input rights, output licence, restrictions and review before release.
music_brief.rhythm_pattern: quarter note alternates with two eighth notes across bars
music_brief.sound_description: Played in rapid unsyncopated two-four time with pentatonic melodies, featuring flutes like the quena and pan flute alongside drums, and sometimes charango or guitar.
music_brief.prompt: Original instrumental composition in the musical world of Cachua (Peru). Meter 2/4. Rhythm pattern: quarter note alternates with two eighth notes across bars. Instruments: quena, pan flute, drums, charango, guitar. Vocal style: singing with repeated verse pairs. Mood: festive, rapid, lively. It should sound like this: Played in rapid unsyncopated two-four time with pentatonic melodies, featuring flutes like the quena and pan flute alongside drums, and sometimes charango or guitar. New melody, new arrangement: do not quote or imitate any specific recorded song; keep the idiom, the instruments, the pulse and the proportions.

tracks.use: chapters: dance it to the music

rules: Original composition only — no sampling, no melody of any existing recording, no lyrics from any song.
Traditional public-domain tunes may be used only when the profile names them and a public-domain source is on file; otherwise compose new material in the idiom.
Keep the proportions true: the meter, the tempo range and the instrument roles the sources describe.
Label every generated track with the tool, the date and this brief, so provenance is always clear.

wardrobe.policy: neutral dress with a respectful nod (palette and fabric only): the sources describe sacred, ceremonial or restricted attire, or the dance is sacred
care: every element traceable to the costume notes or a licensed image; nothing added for effect
no caricature, no exaggeration, no mixing of regions or eras
a culture bearer reviews the wardrobe before production; the review is recorded in the pack
